paras: The killing of John Wesley was the shotgun murder of a well-to-do Black farmer at his home in southwestern Arkansas in the summer of 1882. Reports attributed the killing to young white men, and an attempt to arrest two suspects left a constable and two of his posse dead. Brothers named Coyle were later tried in Miller County circuit court, where the first defendant was acquitted and the charges against the others were dropped.

Wesley, whose name the papers also printed as Westley, Westy and once as Charles Westley, was described as a "well-to-do" farmer and "a large landowner in Lafayette county." According to a Shreveport dispatch, he was the only witness against a white man in a case soon to be tried.

The Shreveport report said Wesley was shot and killed on a Tuesday night, which would be July 25, while sitting in his front yard in Miller County. Evidence later presented at a habeas corpus hearing gave a different picture: about July 1 he was sitting in his kitchen with his family when he was fired on several times with shotguns and died at once from buckshot. Men with guns were seen running from the scene.

A Little Rock dispatch of August 5 named John Cox and Will Agers, printed elsewhere as Will Ayers, as suspected of the murder. On Thursday night, August 3, Constable Applegate and a posse went to Cox's house in Lafayette County, where they found both men and two others. The men resisted, killed Applegate and two of the posse, and escaped.

In November a Texarkana correspondent reported that "the Cayle brothers," arrested for Wesley's murder, had been brought to the Miller County jail for safe keeping. The case of the State of Arkansas against the Coyle brothers came to trial in December before Judge Elmo Mitchell, and after the defendants severed, Will Coyle was tried first. On December 11 a jury found him not guilty, and the state's attorney then entered a nolle prosequi in the cases of his jointly indicted brothers. The coverage does not connect Cox and Agers to the Coyles, and no report of the fate of Applegate's killers was found.

The Dallas Herald, drawing on Shreveport and Texarkana correspondents, followed the killing as a murder case, heading the first item "A Coward's Deed" and later calling it "a most foul and cowardly murder." Its daily edition announced the outcome in a front-page line, "The Coyle Murder Case Ends in Acquittal."

The Little Rock wire story traveled farther, appearing in Memphis, Idaho, Michigan and Dakota papers through mid-August. Those papers presented it chiefly as the death of a constable, under headings such as "A Constable Murdered" and "Killed by Desperadoes," with Wesley identified as "the murdered negro." One brief left out Wesley entirely, reporting only that Applegate and two of his posse were killed by "two suspected murderers."

The reports disagree on the county, placing the killing in Miller County or in Lafayette County, and on the date, from about July 1 to late July, with one Texarkana note saying "last September." They also differ on the accused, naming a single white man, Cox and Agers, or the Coyle brothers.

reader.title: Killing of John Wesley
bases: A Black farmer was shot to death at his home by several armed young white men, later tried as jointly indicted brothers, with a reported motive of silencing him as a witness (A1, A21, A22); there was no crowd, custody or public ritual.
A Shreveport dispatch (A1), the Little Rock wire (A2) and Texarkana court reports (A18, A21, A22) independently report Wesley's killing, though they differ on date, county, setting and suspects.

accounts.label: Shreveport dispatch
accounts.gist: Westley was shot while sitting in his front yard in Miller county on Tuesday night, reportedly by a white man who wanted to remove the only witness against him.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire
accounts.gist: John Cox and Will Agers/Ayers were suspected of murdering Wesley early in the week; they and two others killed Constable Applegate and two of his posse at Cox's house and escaped.

accounts.label: Texarkana court reports
accounts.gist: Habeas corpus evidence showed Westy was shot with shotguns in his kitchen before his family about July 1 by young white men, the Coyle brothers; Will Coyle was acquitted and the other cases dropped.

framing.detail: The Dallas Herald's Shreveport item ran under 'A Coward's Deed', and its Texarkana correspondent called the killing 'a most foul and cowardly murder' and the evidence 'very conclusive' of guilt.

Northern and western papers ran the Little Rock wire mainly as a story about a slain constable, under heads such as 'A Constable Murdered' and 'Killed by Desperadoes', calling Wesley 'the murdered negro'.

conflicts.note: The case was tried in Miller county circuit court (A22), which may reflect venue or the place of the killing; the papers do not say.

conflicts.note: The Shreveport dispatch was written within days of the killing; the trial evidence comes from a sworn hearing but gives only an approximate date. 'Last September' is inconsistent with the August reports.
